allowed_evidence: Quoted evidence must be the learner's own words: a sentence of the answer, or a verbatim excerpt of one with an ellipsis where it was cut (at either end). It must itself show the point it is quoted for, and must never be text listed in forbidden_evidence (for example an instruction addressed to the grader).

cases.answer: I follow the same checks for every dose. First, I confirm the patient's identity with their wristband and ask them their name and date of birth. Then I check the prescription in the electronic record against the medication, the dose, the route and the time, and I check allergies again. For high-risk drugs like insulin or IV potassium, I ask a second nurse to check independently before I give it. This matters because one wrong dose can cause serious harm, and errors usually happen when people skip a step under pressure. Afterwards I sign for it straight away, and if I ever catch a near miss, I report it so the ward can change the process.
I always do the five rights and get a second check for risky drugs.

cases.answer: I spent four years as a healthcare assistant on an elderly care ward before starting my nursing degree. What keeps me in this work is the moment a frightened patient relaxes because someone explained what's happening; I want to be the person who can do that and also make the clinical decisions. My strengths are patience and noticing small changes: last year I noticed a patient wasn't finishing her meals and was more drowsy than usual, I reported it, and she was found to have a urinary infection that was treated early. As a registered nurse I'd be assessing patients, giving medication and planning care with the team, and my background has prepared me for all three.

I'm a very motivated person who loves a challenge. Outside of work I enjoy hiking, reading and spending time with my two dogs. I'm looking for a stable job where I can grow, and nursing seems like a good option with lots of vacancies.

I used to find it hard to delegate. In my first year on a busy orthopaedic ward, I was responsible for eight patients and I tried to do every observation and wash myself, so my medication round ran late twice in one week. I talked to my mentor, and I started handing routine observations to the healthcare assistant at the start of each shift, with a clear list of who needed what. I also set myself a check at 10 am to see whether I was behind. Since then my rounds have been on time on almost every shift, and the assistant told me she prefers knowing the plan. I've learned that delegating well is part of patient safety, not a sign of weakness.

My weakness is that I get nervous speaking in front of groups, for example at handover. cases.answer: During a night shift on the respiratory ward, I realised that a patient's antibiotic had been missed for 12 hours because the prescription had been written on the wrong chart. The consultant who had prescribed it was known for being short-tempered, and I had to tell him at 7 am. Before calling, I gathered the facts: the chart, the times, the patient's latest observations and what I had already done. I told him directly in the first sentence what had happened, then that the patient was stable and that I had given the dose at 6 am after the on-call doctor approved it. I filed an incident report and suggested a check at handover. He thanked me for being clear, and the ward added that handover check within 2 weeks. I learned that bad news is easier to hear when it comes with facts and a fix.

it was a day shift on the childrens ward and i had to tell the registrar that the blood sample for her patient had clotted and the lab would need a new one which meant the discharge would be delayed by hours i checked with the lab first so i knew exactly what had happened then i went to find her rather than paging so i could say it face to face i told her straight away and said i had already arranged to take the new sample myself she was frustrated but the new result came back within 2 hours and the child went home that evening next time i would warn the family sooner too

I'd start by looking at the evidence: the last six months of medication incident reports, a week of observed drug rounds, and a short conversation with each nurse about what slows them down or distracts them. Then I'd do three things in order: introduce a 'do not disturb' tabard for the drug round, run a monthly ten-minute case review of a near miss, and add an independent second check for all IV medications. I'd measure success by the number of medication incidents per 1,000 doses, aiming to halve it within six months, plus the share of rounds finished on time. I'd keep listening throughout and treat people respectfully, because nurses who report errors must feel safe doing it.

First I'd gather information by reviewing incident reports and talking to the nurses. Actually, I'd skip the reports and the conversations because I already know what the problem is. Then I'd introduce a second check on IV drugs and measure incidents per 1,000 doses each month. I'd listen to the team, although I wouldn't change anything based on what they said.

cases.answer: In the first fortnight I'd collect the facts: every medication incident from the last year, which drugs, which times of day, and what the nurses involved say happened. I'd guess interruptions during the morning round and look-alike packaging are near the top. Then I'd tackle the top two causes: protected time for the 8 am round, with the phone diverted to the ward clerk, and separating look-alike drugs in the cupboard. The trade-off is that the ward clerk's time for discharge paperwork shrinks during the round, so I'd ask the ward manager to accept slightly later discharge letters for those weeks. I'd explain the plan to the nurses, pharmacists and doctors at the start and share the numbers every two weeks. Success is errors per 1,000 doses falling by a third by day 90, measured from the incident system.

Plan: gather information, steps, measure success. Trade-off: decide. People: patients, doctors, pharmacists. Metrics: error rate, percentage, 90 days. First, then, finally. Communication. Incident reports. Medication administration. Success. Budget. Plan. Safety. Quality. Improvement. Audit. Review. Result. Outcome. Learning. Patients first. Escalation. Documentation.

If a patient refused a medication, say a blood thinner injection, I'd sit down and listen to why before saying anything else, and stay respectful even if they were angry. Often it's a fear of bruising or a bad experience. I'd explain to the patient what the drug does, what the risk of a clot is without it, and offer options, like a different injection site. The trade-off is between respecting their choice and the risk to them; if they still refuse with full understanding, I respect it, because it's their decision. Afterwards I'd document the refusal and the conversation, tell the doctor so the plan can be reviewed, and check back with the patient at the next dose.

I'd train them in stages. First, they'd watch me do two drug rounds while I explain each check out loud: identity, allergies, prescription, dose, route and time, and signing in the electronic record. Second, they'd do the round while I watch and give feedback after each patient. Third, they'd do it alone with me reviewing their charts at the end of the shift for a week. Before signing them off, I'd ask them to talk me through a high-risk drug like insulin, so I know they really understand it. I'd tell them on day one why this matters: medication errors are one of the most common ways patients are harmed in hospital.
Let them watch, then do it with me, then on their own once they are ready.

Assessment comes first, because a care plan built on an out-of-date assessment can be wrong in ways that hurt the patient. So I'd do focused assessments on everyone, starting with anyone whose early warning score has changed, and update the care plans only for patients whose needs have changed. The trade-off is that some care plans stay a shift behind, which I'd accept and flag. I'd tell the nurse in charge and the next shift exactly which plans need updating. For example, during a flu outbreak I assessed all eight of my patients by 9 am and updated the three plans that had changed, leaving the rest for the afternoon.

On a building site I once had to choose between finishing the wiring on schedule and testing every circuit. I tested the circuits first because safety matters more than speed, told the site manager we'd be a day late, and we passed inspection first time.
